title: TA9-04015
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Mexico, seeks refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the IRPA).1 The claimant's identity has been established through a certified copy of the claimant's passport.2 ALLEGATIONS
The claimant alleged that on XXXXX, 2008, sometime between 3:00-4:00 PM, he was at the office of the XXXXX XXXXX he worked for which XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. The office has a company telephone.

He heard a knock at the door. He looked out and saw three men, two of them standing beside a black pick-up truck without license plates and they were wearing dark glasses. The other man was standing at the door knocking. He did not know these men.

The claimant answered the door and the man standing there asked him if this was XXXXX XXXXX home, the claimant's neighbour. The claimant told him no and the man, who thought the claimant was lying, got angry and started to swear at him. The man threatened the claimant and demanded that he open the door and let him in. The claimant refused and the man went to the next door.

The claimant alleged that he saw the three men dragging his neighbour and pushed him into the car. The claimant said the man who was knocking his door pulled out a gun and threatened him not to say anything or he would be killed. Other neigbours started to come out of their homes and the claimant alleged that the men sped off in their car with the neighbour.
The claimant said he phoned the police and made a report of the incident.

On XXXXX 2008, he saw an article in the newspaper that human remains were found in different places in the city and that one of them was his neighbour who he had witnessed being dragged from his home. The claimant alleged that he called the police hotline which is set up for anonymous callers to make confidential reports and reported what he had observed on XXXXX, 2008.

On XXXXX, 2008, the claimant alleged that he heard a knock on his door and, peeking out, he saw a man he recognized as one of the kidnappers who had taken his neighbour away. The claimant also alleged that he overheard the man talking on his cell phone that he would kill the claimant, after which he slipped a note under the claimant's door. The note threatened to kill the claimant and that he should not contact the police. It was also signed by XXXXX.

Realizing he was being threatened by drug gangsters, the claimant further alleged that he left the area, his job and belongings and went to live in the city of XXXXX where he found a job. The claimant alleged that he was found and he moved to two other locations where he was also found.
The claimant alleged that he applied for a visa to the United States but was denied, so he came to Canada on February 24, 2009 and filed for refugee protection on XXXXX, 2009.

The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. The claimant does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention reason and his removal to Mexico would not subject him personally to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture.

In arriving at my decision, the panel considered the issue of whether the claimant's fear is objectively reasonable. In this regard, the panel considered whether or not there is adequate state protection in Mexico, whether the claimant took all reasonable steps to avail himself of that protection, and whether he has provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. ANALYSIS State Protection and Credibility

The Board, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by a number of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. The courts have established a number of principles relating to state protection and the panel has applied those principles to the case at hand.

There is a presumption that, except in situations where the state is in complete breakdown, the state is capable of protecting its citizens. The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available.3

A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that the evidence establishes that the state protection is inadequate. To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide "clear and convincing" evidence of the state's inability to protect its citizens. The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.4 Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that the state's efforts are not always successful will not rebut the presumption of state protection.5 A claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state.6 Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when one has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of a presumption of state protection.7

Refugee protection is meant to be a form of surrogate protection to be invoked only in those situations where the refugee claimant has unsuccessfully sought the protections of his home state. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.8 In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim, at least where the state is a functioning democracy with a willingness and the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.9

The claimant's burden of proof is directly proportional to the level of democracy in the state in question: the more democratic the state's institutions, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all courses of action open to them.10 In a functioning democracy, a claimant will have a heavy burden when attempting to show that they should not have been required to exhaust all of the recourses available to them domestically before claiming refugee status.11 The claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. A claimant must show that they have taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken and the claimant's interactions with the authorities.12 Local failures by authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of the state's inability or refusal to provide protection.13

In view of these principles, the panel finds that the claimant has not provided clear and convincing evidence, that on a balance of probabilities, state protection in Mexico is inadequate. In this particular case, the claimant was questioned as to what efforts he made to seek state protection. He testified that he witnessed his neighbour being dragged from his home and placed into a pick-up truck by three men. On XXXXX, 2008, from the newspaper, he later learned that bodies were found in different parts of the cities and one of those bodies was his neighbour's who he had witnessed being dragged from his home on XXXXX, 2008. The claimant testified that on XXXXX, 2008 he called the emergency call service which is set up for citizens to anonymously call and report crimes they may have witnessed. He reported the incident he had witnessed.

However, the claimant testified that on XXXXX 2008, someone who he recognized as one of the men who had dragged away his neighbour was at his door knocking. He did not open the door but overheard the man talking on his cell-phone that he was going to kill the claimant. The man also slid a note under the claimant's door which stated that they already knew who the claimant was and he should not open his mouth about anything he had heard or seen or he would be killed. The note was signed XXXXX XXXXX The claimant did not report the incident to the police. Instead, he said he left his job, his belongings and fled to XXXXX, XXXXX, where he found a new job. He also said he threw away the note. However, the claimant testified that he had a friend who was a sergeant in the municipal police force. The claimant was asked why he did not report the incident to his police friend. He said because his friend could not help him too much. However, the claimant testified that he did mention the incident to this police friend in an informal way and he told him to watch himself for these were heavy duty guys and dangerous. The claimant was asked why he did not include the conversation with his police friend in his Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative or his amended narrative.14. He said at that moment he didn't consider including the conversation in his narrative because it was a very short conversation. However, the panel believes the fact that the claimant considered it worthy to mention this conversation with a police officer who informed him that the people who threatened him are heavy duty and dangerous and he should be careful, to the panel, is because he thinks it is relevant information and which goes to the basis of his subjective and objective fear. The panel therefore believes if he had had that conversation with a police officer who told him to be careful because the men who threatened him are dangerous, he would have included it in his narrative. The panel notes that the claimant is represented by counsel and he, with the help of counsel, had previously amended his narrative.15 Therefore, the panel finds that this omission undermines the claimant's credibility.

Therefore, the claimant's testimony that he was threatened that he would be killed by drug gangsters that was contained in a written note that was slid under his door, the panel does not believe. For example, the claimant was asked where the threatening note that was slid under his door was. In response, the claimant asked, at the present time? He was told yes, and he said he did not conserve it. He was asked what he did with the note, and he said he threw it away. Asked why he threw the note away, the claimant said that he got so frightened he started to think about the problems and how to get out of them. So he was asked again, why did he throw the note away. At that point the claimant said he did not think he would need it, as he did not think he would be coming to Canada.

The panel believes that the claimant was making up the story as he went along in respect to the alleged note. The panel notes that when he was first asked about the note, his response was, at the present time? The claimant did not just say he didn't have it because he threw it away. He enquired if the panel wanted to know where the note was at this time as if there was another time the panel could have wanted to know where the note was. The panel finds the claimant's answer evasive, vague and confusing and further finds that on a balance of probability there is no threatening note. The note is a fabrication to bolster his claim for refugee status.

The panel notes that the foundation of the claimant's claim is based on the threatening note he alleged he received. The panel notes that it has an obligation to be satisfied that the evidence it relies on is probably so, not possibly so.16 The panel finds no persuasive evidence before it that the claimant's allegations are probably so, and not possibly so, especially in the absence of corroborative documents, such as the note which is central to his allegation that he was being threatened. For example, where a claimant's story has been found to be implausible or otherwise lacking in credibility, as in this case, this panel finds a lack of documentary corroboration to be a valid consideration in assessing the claimant's credibility17 or a lack of efforts to obtain the documentation.18 It is therefore reasonable for the panel to attach great importance to documentation which would have supported the allegations.19

The panel reminds itself that it is entitled to rely on documentary evidence in preference to the testimony provided by the claimant,20 even if it finds the claimant trustworthy and credible.21 However, the panel also notes the caution that the Federal Court has provided to the panel in taking this approach.22

But even if the claimant was threatened, and the panel does not believe he was, state protection exists in Mexico. The panel carefully examined the evidence before it in light of several rulings from the Federal Court. For example, the claimant must show that he has taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken and his interactions with the authorities.23 The panel finds that he made absolutely no efforts to approach the state for protection; and finds that his explanation for not taking all reasonable steps to seek state protection was not compelling, for it is based on speculation that they would hurt him. The Federal Court states that in the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim, at least where the state is a functioning democracy with a willingness and the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens24. There is no persuasive evidence before it that Mexico is a failed state. So, doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when the claimant has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of a presumption of state protection.25

The panel also takes into account the Federal Court ruling that the adequacy of state protection cannot rest on the subjective fear of the claimant.26 A claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state27 (see also Camacho28).

The Federal Court has held that a claimant's decision to flee before police have had an opportunity to properly respond to and investigate a transgression did not amount to a lack of state protection.29 In this particular case, there is no information to suggest that police would not make genuine and earnest efforts to investigate the claimant's allegations and apprehend the perpetrators if the claimant had reported the incidents to the police and in the case of the one incident the police was made aware of, if the claimant had followed up. The claimant's choice to leave Mexico may have resulted in the investigation being delayed or stymied, given that he, as the victim, was a key witness.

Further, the panel considered the claimant's efforts to report any of this information to any other authority and finds that the claimant did not approach any other authorities; he simply left Mexico.

The claimant was questioned about his views on state protection in Mexico. The claimant responded that the police in Mexico are corrupt. For example, police offers' loyalty is divided among different groups of drug traffickers. The panel finds the claimant's responses regarding the effectiveness of state protection to be not objectively well-founded since they were largely unsubstantiated and contradict the documentary evidence

Further, the panel considered the claimant's efforts to report any of this information to any other authority. He said that as far as he is aware the police forces in Mexico are involved with drug dealers and he cannot guess which police officer is honest. He also said that AFI was very corrupt. The claimant based his belief on what he has gathered from the media. When he was asked about the Human Rights Commission, he said that they did not have a big influence in Mexico. Asked why they don't have a big influence, he said they will not investigate cases because they too can be threatened.

The claimant was questioned about his views on state protection in Mexico. The claimant responded that he does not trust any level of police in Mexico because the majority of the police in Mexico are corrupt. The panel found the claimant's responses regarding the effectiveness of state protection to be not objectively well-founded since they were largely unsubstantiated and contradict the documentary evidence. The panel would be remiss if it did not acknowledge and consider that there is information in the documentation to indicate that inefficiency, bribery and corruption remain issues in Mexican security forces at all levels, as well as within the public service sector. However, weighted against this is persuasive evidence that indicates that Mexico candidly acknowledges its past problems and is making serious efforts to rectify the corruption and impunity that exists.

The documentary evidence30 before the Board indicates that Mexico is a functioning democracy, and there are free and fair elections. There is a relatively independent and impartial judiciary. Having canvassed the country conditions documents, the panel finds that Mexico is in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country. There are "about 400,000 police officers in the country and about 3,000 different forces at municipal, state and federal levels."31 There is nothing in the documentary evidence before the Board to suggest that Mexico is in a state of complete breakdown.

The Board accepts that Mexico has had some difficulties in the past with addressing the criminality and corruption that exists within the security forces in Mexico. The Board recognizes that there are some inconsistencies among several sources within the documentary evidence; however, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is an adequate state protection in Mexico for victims of crime, that Mexico is making serious efforts to address the problem of criminality, and that the police are both willing and able to protect victims. Police corruption and deficiencies, although existing and noted by the Board, are not systemic. The panel is of the view in canvassing the documentary evidence, that, as a whole, the issues of corruption and deficiencies are being addressed by the state of Mexico. Corruption and inefficiency plague the Mexican police. In addition, low pay and lack of resources have hindered efforts at improving police performance, battling corruption, and professionalizing the forces. ... In more recent nationwide polls, only 12 percent of the population has expressed confidence in the police. In response to this crisis of public confidence, President Fox made reducing public corruption a key goal of his administration, and he gained international recognition for his efforts.32

For instance, The Mexican government has introduced a number of significant reforms in its security forces to combat crime over the past number of years: First, the federal Office of the Attorney General (PGR) recently established a new police force, the Federal Investigative Police (AFI) which replaced the notoriously corrupt Federal Judicial Police (PJF). ... Efforts to develop the AFI into a professional, corruption-free force for the investigation of federal crimes are ongoing. Second, the Federal Preventive Police (PFP) was created in 1999 ... to prevent and combat crime throughout the country. The PFP came under the direction of the federal Ministry of Public Security (SSP) and has been assuming greater authority in stages over time, as its budget has grown and as it has incorporated and reorganized police departments from other major agencies such as those for migration, treasury, and highways. Third, the Public Security Secretariat of the federal District (SSP-DF) unlike the PFP and SSP, does not have national reach, but it does manage a combined force of over 90,000 officers in the Federal District (DF). The SSP-DF is charged with maintaining public order and safety in the centre of Mexico City, where public insecurity and crime rates are the highest in the nation. As a result, there have been concurrent efforts to increase accountability and improve police effectiveness. ... The most high-profile effort was Mexico City Mayor Andrés Obrador's decision in 2002 to contract former New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani as a consultant to the SSP-DF.33

Furthermore, starting in the previous decade, Mexico created a number of agencies to combat crime, the drug cartels and organized crime: First, the PGR's Special Anti-Organized Crime Unit (UEDO) appeared as a response to the phenomenon of organized crime. ... The Federal Law against Organized Crime (LFCDO) was passed in November 1996 to deal with the problem of drug trafficking, though other crimes (such as migrant smuggling, trafficking in arms or infants, and terrorism) were covered in the LFCDO as well. Second, another unit within the PGR that has been important in the effort to combat drug tr4afficking and organized crime is the Office of the Special Prosecutor for Crimes against Health (FEADS). ... A third special office of the PGR is the Office of the Deputy Attorney for Special Investigation of Organized Crime (SIEDO) ... As currently organized, SIEDO contains six special units for investigating specific types of crimes: crimes against public health; terrorism and arms trafficking; money laundering and counterfeiting; human trafficking in minors, organs, and undocumented people; kidnappings; and robber and other theft. ... The special offices of the PGR demonstrate the general rule that Mexican policing institutions try to reorganize themselves in a rational way to respond effectively to specific crime problems.34

There is documentary evidence35 that persons who face police misconduct, inefficiency or corruption can ask the Secretariat of the Public Administration (SFP), the Program Against Impunity, or the Office of the Attorney General (PGR) to investigate federal and state police failures or misconduct.

Documentary evidence36 indicates that efforts to ensure police effectiveness and purge corruption include investigations by the Secretary of Public Security, complaints monitored by the Inspector General, and a 24-hour hotline to report corrupt officials.

Further documentary evidence indicates that the security forces have instituted new recruiting procedures, drug testing, economic incentives, education and certification of officers, with sanctions levied against ineffective or corrupt officers, including arrests, prosecutions and convictions of members of the security forces. The new government laws attacking corruption and bribery have resulted in sentences of five to 10 years' imprisonment for convicted officials, which have reportedly had a marked effect.37

In view of the above-mentioned principles and when considering the Board's documentary evidence weighted against the claimant's evidence, the panel finds that the claimant, in the circumstances of this case, has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence and that the claimant did not take all reasonable steps in the circumstances to avail himself of that protection before making a claim for refugee protection. Therefore, the panel is not persuaded that the state of Mexico would not be reasonably forthcoming with state protection, should the claimant seek it.

For all these reasons, the panel finds that that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, whether under section 96 or section 97 of the Act, as state protection is available to huim.

The panel determines that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim.
